entries.title: printf
entries.summary: Print formatted text to standard output.
entries.description: The format is plain text plus conversions `%[flags][width][.precision][length]conversion`. Each conversion consumes one argument, which must match its type. Returns the number of characters printed.

details.name: %d %i
details.text: signed int (`%ld` long, `%lld` long long, `%hd` short)

details.name: %x %X
details.text: unsigned int in hexadecimal (lower / upper case)

details.name: %f
details.text: double in decimal notation; `%.2f` prints 2 decimals

details.name: flags
details.text: `-` left-justify, `+` always show the sign, `0` pad with zeros, space = space before positive numbers

details.name: width
details.text: `%5d` pads to at least 5 characters; `%*d` takes the width from an argument

mistakes: `%d` with a `size_t`, `long` or double argument: use `%zu`, `%ld`, `%f`.
Passing user text as the format (`printf(s)`): write `printf("%s", s)`.

entries.title: fprintf
entries.summary: Print formatted text to a stream (a file, stdout or stderr).
entries.description: Same formats as `printf`, but the first argument says where to write: `stdout`, `stderr` or a `FILE *` from `fopen`. Errors belong on `stderr` so they stay visible when the output is redirected.
entries.example:
fprintf(stderr, "%s: %s\n", path, strerror(errno));
fprintf(f, "%d %s\n", id, name);
mistakes: Printing error messages with printf: they get mixed into the normal output.

entries.title: snprintf
entries.summary: Format into a string, never writing more than n bytes.
entries.syntax: int snprintf(char *buf, size_t n, const char *format, …);
entries.description: Writes at most `n - 1` characters and always terminates the string. Returns the length the full result would have had, so a value `>= n` means it was truncated. Prefer it to `sprintf`.
entries.example:
char path[256];
snprintf(path, sizeof(path), "%s/%s", dir, name);
mistakes: Passing `strlen(buf)` instead of the buffer size as `n`.

entries.title: sprintf
entries.summary: Format into a string (unchecked: can overflow the buffer).
entries.description: Like `printf` but the result goes into `buf`, which must be large enough: nothing checks it. Use `snprintf` in new code.
mistakes: Buffer overflow when the result is longer than the buffer.

entries.title: scanf
entries.summary: Read formatted input from standard input; every argument is an address.
entries.description: Returns the number of items successfully assigned, or `EOF` if the input ended before the first conversion: always check it. Whitespace in the format (and before `%d`, `%f`, `%s`) skips any amount of whitespace; `%c` does not skip (write `" %c"`). `%d` reads an int, `%ld` a long, `%f` a float, `%lf` a double, `%s` a word, `%c` a character. `%s` stops at whitespace: give it a width (`%9s` for a `char[10]`).
mistakes: Forgetting the `&`: `scanf("%d", n)` writes to a random address.
Using `%f` for a double (it must be `%lf`).

entries.title: sscanf
entries.summary: Read formatted values from a string.
entries.description: Like `scanf` but reads from `str`. Often used after `fgets` to parse a line safely. Returns the number of items assigned.

entries.title: fscanf
entries.summary: Read formatted input from a file.
entries.description: Like `scanf` on a stream. Returns the number of items assigned, or `EOF` at the end of the file. A loop such as `while (fscanf(f, "%63s", word) == 1)` reads word by word.
mistakes: Testing `!feof(f)` instead of the return value.

entries.title: getchar
entries.summary: Read one character from standard input.
entries.description: Returns the character as an `int` (0 to 255) or `EOF` (-1) at the end of the input or on error: store the result in an `int`, not a `char`.

entries.title: putchar
entries.summary: Write one character to standard output.
entries.description: Writes `c` converted to an unsigned char. Returns the character written or `EOF` on error.

entries.title: puts
entries.summary: Write a string followed by a newline to standard output.
entries.description: Unlike `fputs`, it adds the newline. Returns a non-negative number on success or `EOF`.

entries.title: gets
entries.summary: Read a line into a buffer WITHOUT a size limit (removed in C11: never use it).
entries.description: It cannot know the buffer size, so any long line overflows it. Use `fgets`.

entries.title: fgets
entries.summary: Read a line, at most size - 1 characters.
entries.description: Reads up to `size - 1` characters, stopping after a newline, and always terminates the buffer with `'\0'`. The newline, if read, stays in the buffer. Returns `buf`, or NULL at the end of the file or on error. A line longer than the buffer comes in several pieces: a piece that does not end in `'\n'` (and is not the end of the file) is the start of a longer line.
mistakes: Counting a long line as several lines.
Forgetting that the newline is part of the data.

entries.title: fputs
entries.summary: Write a string to a stream, without adding a newline.
entries.description: Returns a non-negative number on success or `EOF`. Use `fprintf` when you need formatting.

entries.title: fgetc
entries.summary: Read one character from a stream.
entries.description: Returns the character as an `int`, or `EOF` at the end of the file or on error. `getc` is the same call (it may be a macro).

entries.title: fputc
entries.summary: Write one character to a stream.
entries.syntax:
int fputc(int c, FILE *stream);
int putc(int c, FILE *stream);
entries.description: Returns the character written or `EOF` on error. `putc` is the same call (it may be a macro).

entries.title: perror
entries.summary: Print your message followed by the text of the last error to stderr.
entries.description: Prints `prefix: message` and a newline, using the current value of `errno`. Call it right after the failing call.
mistakes: Calling another function between the failure and `perror`.

entries.title: stdin
entries.summary: The three standard streams: stdin (0), stdout (1) and stderr (2).
entries.description: Already open in every process. stdin reads the keyboard (or a pipe/file), stdout writes the normal output, stderr writes errors and is not buffered. The shell can redirect them: `prog > out.txt 2> err.txt < in.txt`. As file descriptors they are 0, 1 and 2.
